title: Have you heard the cuckoo?
translation: A man who can answer a woman on the spot, and get it right, is rare. In Emperor Kameyama's day, some mischievous court ladies used to test the young nobles as they arrived at the palace. They'd ask each one: "Have you heard the cuckoo yet?" One major counsellor answered, "A nobody like me hasn't had the chance." The Horikawa Inner Minister said, "I believe I may have heard one at Iwakura." The ladies talked it over and decided: "That one's fine. 'A nobody like me' is a bit much."

People say you should bring a boy up so that women won't laugh at him. The Jōdoji regent was taught well by Ankimon'in when he was small, and that's why he spoke so nicely, they said. And the Yamashina Minister of the Left once said, "Even when some lowly maid sees me, I feel shy and watch what I do."
If there were no women in the world, nobody would bother to straighten his robes or his cap.

You'd think that women, who make men so careful, must be wonderful. But women are all crooked by nature. They cling to themselves and they're terribly greedy. They don't understand how things are. Their minds go straight to whatever leads them astray. They're good with words, but ask them something harmless and they won't answer. Just when you think they're discreet, they come out with shocking things nobody asked about. They scheme and dress things up so cleverly you'd think they were smarter than men, but they never see that it will all come out later. A woman is crooked, and a fool.

Trying to please a mind like that, to be well thought of, is miserable. So why be shy in front of a woman? And if there were a wise woman, she'd be distant and cold too. Women only seem sweet and charming when you let desire run you and do what they want.

literal: Saying that a man who makes a reply to a woman's remark promptly and suitably is a rare thing,
in the time of the Kameyama Retired Emperor, mischievous court ladies, each time young men came to the palace, tested them by asking, 'Have you heard the cuckoo?';
a certain major counsellor, it seems, answered, 'One who does not count has not been able to hear it.'
The Horikawa Inner Minister said, 'I believe I heard it at Iwakura',
(and) they judged together, 'This has no fault. "One who does not count" is awkward.'
'Men in general should be brought up so as not to be laughed at by women,' (it is said), and
the former regent of Jōdoji, because Ankimon'in taught him well when he was young, had good speech and the like, someone said, I hear.
The Yamashina Minister of the Left said, 'Even when a lowly maid looks at me, I feel very shy and am careful.'
If it were a world without women, no one would set right their robes and caps, however they might be.
When I think how splendid women must be, before whom people feel so shy, (I find that) woman's nature is all twisted.

The mark of self is deep in them, their greed is great, they do not know the principles of things, their minds move quickly only in the direction of delusion, their words are skilful, and when one asks even about something harmless they do not say;
when one thinks they are discreet, again they bring out even shocking things unasked.
When one thinks that the things they plot deeply and dress up are superior even to the wisdom of men, they do not know that the matter will come out afterwards.
What is not straightforward and is foolish: that is woman.
To follow such a mind and wish to be thought well of would surely be miserable.
So why should one feel shy before a woman?
If there were a wise woman, she too would surely be distant and cold.
Only when one takes delusion as one's master and follows them should they seem gentle and delightful.

notes.text: Emperor Kameyama (1249–1305), who reigned from 1259 to 1274 and then ruled for some years as retired emperor.
しれたる: from しる 'to be silly, to fool around'; here 'playful, mischievous'. Not modern {知|し}れた 'well-known'.

The cuckoo ({時鳥|ほととぎす}) arrives in early summer, and hearing its first call was a favourite subject of poems. People stayed up at night to hear it. So the question is a test of a man's poetic manners, not of his ears.
'One who does not count': a stock humble phrase from poetry. The ladies find it {難|むつか}し, 'awkward, too much'. The minister's answer is modest without making a show of it.
Probably Horikawa Tomomori (1249–1316). Kenkō is thought to have served the Horikawa family as a young man. {岩倉|いはくら}: a hill village north of Kyoto. やらむ: 'perhaps, I think', a soft hedge.
Usually identified as Kujō Moronori (died 1320), a former regent; some commentators say his father Tadanori. Ankimon'in was the consort of Emperor Go-Horikawa (reigned 1221–1232).
Usually identified as Tōin Saneo (died 1273), Minister of the Left in the early 1260s.
ひがむ: 'to be twisted, warped' + り. Modern ひがむ means 'to be resentful, jealous'. From here the section turns from court gossip into a sermon.

notes.quote: 人我の相ふかく、貪欲甚だしく
notes.text: The list of faults is in Buddhist language: {人我|にんが}, clinging to the idea of a self; {貪欲|とんよく}, greed, one of the three poisons; {迷|まよ}ひ, delusion. Buddhist texts of the time often described women this way. Compare sections 8 and 9 on desire.

notes.quote: ただ迷ひをあるじとしてかれに随ふ時
notes.text: The closing: women seem 'gentle and delightful' only to a man ruled by delusion. べし: 'it is natural that…'. The section began with men trying not to be laughed at by women and ends by saying there is nothing to be shy about.
